summary: Joseph Haekel completed his Ph.D. at the University of Vienna (1931–1935). He remained there as assistant to Koppers in 1935, PD in 1941, and ordinary professor and director in 1957, succeeding Wilhelm Koppers.

Working in religious studies and philosophy, Haroutunian studied at the American University of Beirut, Columbia University (Ph.D. c. 1928–1932), and Union Theological Seminary. He taught at Wellesley College, McCormick Theological Seminary, and the University of Chicago (1962–1968).

Specializing in Indology and linguistics, Wyatt studied at St Augustine's College, Canterbury, and Christ's College, Cambridge (M.A. c. 1883–1893). In 1895, he served as a university teacher at the University of Cambridge.

Loizzo, active in Buddhist studies, philosophy, and Tibetology, studied at Amherst College and Harvard University under Robert A. F. Thurman and Tsenshab Serkong Rinpoche. Attested in 2007, he founded the Nalanda Institute and served as a visiting scholar at Columbia University.

Kitagawa studied at Rikkyo University and the University of Chicago (Ph.D. c. 1947–1951 under Joachim Wach). A religious studies scholar, he taught at Chicago from 1951 to 1984, serving as Dean of the Divinity School.

Linguist and Indologist Joseph Mansion studied at Ghent University (Ph.D. 1894–1899) under Louis de La Vallée Poussin. He succeeded Charles Michel in 1908 and held posts at the University of Liège from 1904, becoming extraordinary professor in 1910.
Philosopher Joseph Margolis earned his M.A. from Columbia University (c. 1947–1950). In 1991, he held the Laura H. Carnell Chair of Philosophy at Temple University.

Marino, an Indology and Buddhist studies scholar, earned M.A. degrees from Ohio State University and the University of Washington, studying under Collett Cox and Richard G. Salomon. He became an assistant professor at the University of Washington in 2020.

Masson studied at Jesuit College, Leuven, and KU Leuven (doctorate 1942). In Indology and religious studies, he taught at Saint-Robert Bellarmin, the University of Namur, and was appointed Professor of Buddhism and Mission Theology at the Pontifical Gregorian University in 1958.
Indologist Joseph Menrad earned his Ph.D. from the University of Munich. He later served as school director at the Willibald-Gymnasium from 1921 to 1926.

Working in Indology, Merkel taught Franz Bopp and held posts as a teacher at Karls-Universität Aschaffenburg (1810), professor at Gymnasium Aschaffenburg (1818), and court librarian at Hofbibliothek Aschaffenburg (1828).

Active in Indology and religious studies, Mullens studied at Coward College, the University of London (B.A. c. 1838–1841), Williams College, and the University of Edinburgh. In 1865, he became foreign secretary for the London Missionary Society.

Rawson studied at Jesus College, Oxford (c. 1908–1912) under Arthur Anthony Macdonell and J. N. Farquhar. In Indology, philosophy, and religious studies, he was professor at Serampore College (c. 1913–1940) and a fellow at the University of Calcutta.

Needham studied at the University of Cambridge and Gonville and Caius College. Active in sinology and history/archaeology, he was a fellow at Caius, Reader in Biochemistry at Cambridge (c. 1933–1966), and director of the Needham Research Institute (c. 1976–1990).
Working in Indology and linguistics, Peet studied at the Church Missionary Society College, Islington in 1829. He later served as principal of CMS College Kottayam from around 1835 to 1840.

Prabhu studied under John N. Findlay, Bernard Williams, and Alasdair MacIntyre. Active in philosophy, religious studies, and Indology, he held posts at California State University, Los Angeles, and was a visiting professor at UCSB, UTC Bangalore, and Bossey.

Ratzinger studied at the University of Munich and Ducal Georgianum. In religious studies, he held academic posts at Munich (1958–1959), Bonn (1959–1963), Münster (1963–1966), Tübingen (1966–1969), and Regensburg (1969–1977).

Active in sinology and Tibetology, Rock taught at Mills College, served as botanist at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa (1908; 1911–1920), worked for the USDA, and held a post at the Harvard-Yenching Institute (1946–1949).
Indologist Joseph Rupp studied at the University of Munich from around 1840 to 1844. He later served as a gymnasium professor at Dom-Gymnasium Freising from 1850 to 1882.
Alter, active in Indology and religious studies, completed his Ph.D. at the University of California, Berkeley. Attested in 2008, he held a post as professor at the University of Pittsburgh.
